newsitem.title: USA: US bonds end a bit higher before retail sales data.
newsitem.headline: US bonds end a bit higher before retail sales data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended a bit higher on Monday after profit-taking erased most of an early advance based on expectations for weak economic data, analysts said.

"The market was just not willing to make a bold move until we see the numbers this week and get a clearer idea of what the Federal Reserve is likely to do next week (at its May 20 Federal Open Market Committee policy meeting)," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
The benchmark 30-year bond closed up 2/32 at 96-22/32 to yield 6.89 percent.
Meanwhile, two-year notes ended at 100-9/32, up 1/32 to yield 6.22 percent. Five-year notes closed at 100-16/32, up 3/32 to yield 6.50 percent.

The market got scant fresh economic news on Monday but climbed, nonetheless, on expectations that several substantive economic reports due later in the week would show that the economy weakened in April. Such news could be expected to comfort bond investors who live in fear that a robust economy eventually will spark inflation.

On Tuesday, the government is expected to report that retail sales weakened in April. Economists polled by Reuters, on average, said sales fell 0.3 percent during the month and rose 0.1 percent with auto sales removed from the equation.

"We've seen two of the retail sales report components already and neither was very strong," said Ram Bhagavatula, chief financial economist at Citicorp Global Finance. "Motor vehicles were actually down and that will pull down the total. Chain-store sales were ho-hum."
Bhagavatula looks for a 0.4 percent retail sales decline and a 0.1 percent increase when auto sales are excluded.

Bhagavatula said economic data set for release this week ought to be helpful to the market. But he noted that the market has been anticipating these reports for two weeks -- ever since the first-quarter Employment Cost Index came in lower than expected and durable goods orders for February and March were weaker than forecast -- and that prices have risen accordingly.

"Prices have moved higher to reflect the view that demand is slowing down and inflation is not a problem," said Bhagavatula. "Thus, if the economic numbers are stronger than expected, the market will give back some of its gains."

Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc., agreed that the market has recently benefitted from the expectation "that the data coming out over the next few days should basically be friendly."

Besides the retail sales report due on Tuesday, the market gets the April Producer Price Index (PPI) on Wednesday and the Consumer Price Index (CPI) on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, that the PPI was unchanged in April and that without its more volatile food and energy items, it would be up 0.1 percent. The CPI is expected to be up 0.1 percent and up 0.2 pct without food and energy items.
Many economists think the April slowdown in retail sales temporary, a view that could help limit the market's ability to advance further on weak data.

"My guess is that weak April retail sales are a matter of consumers catching their breath after six months of spending," said Lieberman. Economists also said income tax payments in April subtracted from consumers' disposable income.

On Monday, three- and six-month bill rates ended unchanged at 5.03 percent and 5.25 percent, respectively. Year bill rates eased one basis point to 5.52 percent. Ten-year notes rose 1/32 to 99-23/32, yielding 6.66 percent.
